cards.front: What is a chromosome?
cards.back: A thread in the nucleus, the cell's inner compartment, that carries the cell's instructions (DNA).
cards.quote: threads in the nucleus, the cell's inner compartment, that carry its instructions (DNA)

cards.front: A typical human body cell that has a nucleus has {{c1::46}} chromosomes.
cards.quote: A typical human body cell that has a nucleus has 46.

cards.front: How do new cells help a living thing grow and heal?
cards.back: When you grow, existing cells divide and the number of cells goes up. When you heal, new cells from dividing replace the ones you lost.
cards.quote: When you grow, the number of cells in your body goes up; when you heal, new cells replace the ones you lost.

cards.front: The {{c1::cell cycle}} is a cell's steps from when it forms until it divides.
cards.back: Its two main parts are interphase and mitosis.
cards.quote: The cell cycle is a cell's steps from when it forms until it divides.

cards.front: What does a cell do during interphase?
cards.back: It grows and copies its chromosomes.
cards.quote: Interphase is when the cell grows and copies its chromosomes.

cards.front: Each new cell is a {{c1::daughter cell}}; the cell that divided is the parent cell.
cards.quote: Each new cell is a daughter cell; the cell that divided is the parent cell.

cards.front: Use a recipe book to explain why a cell copies its chromosomes before it divides.
cards.back: Tear a book in half and each person gets half the recipes. Copy it first and each person gets the whole book. Copying each chromosome first gives each daughter cell the full set.
cards.quote: Tear it in half, and each person gets half the recipes. Copy it first, and each person gets the whole book.

cards.front: In a stained cell, how can you tell prophase from metaphase?
cards.back: Prophase: thick, coiled chromosomes, scattered, not in a row. Metaphase: chromosomes lined up in a row across the middle.
cards.why: The four stages of mitosis come in this order: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase.
cards.quote: Thick, coiled chromosomes, scattered, not in a row.
cards.section: Explain: spotting the four stages of mitosis

cards.front: A photo of a dividing cell shows two matching groups of chromosomes pulled to opposite ends. Which stage is it, and what does the pulling?
cards.back: Anaphase. Thin fibers in the cell pull the chromosomes apart.
cards.quote: thin fibers in the cell do the pulling in anaphase
cards.section: Explain: spotting the four stages of mitosis

cards.front: Why can't a plant cell pinch in two in telophase, and what happens instead?
cards.back: Its stiff wall stops it from pinching in two. A new wall forms across its middle instead.
cards.quote: a plant cell, with its stiff wall, cannot pinch in two in telophase; a new wall forms across its middle instead.
cards.section: Explain: spotting the four stages of mitosis

cards.front: A model cell has 4 chromosomes: red, blue, green and yellow. It skips the copying step and then divides. What does each new cell get?
cards.back: Each gets only 2, for example red and blue in one, green and yellow in the other. Each cell misses two whole chromosomes and their instructions. (A made-up test, not normal mitosis.)
cards.why: Each new cell needs the right number, one of every kind. Without copying, no split gives both cells all four.
cards.quote: Each cell misses two whole chromosomes and their instructions; no split gives both cells all four colours.
cards.section: Explain: spotting the four stages of mitosis

cards.front: A human body cell with 46 chromosomes copies them and divides by mitosis. How many chromosomes does each daughter cell get, and which ones?
cards.back: 46 each: one of every chromosome, the same full set as the parent cell.
cards.why: Copy first, then share: each chromosome is copied, and one copy of each goes to each new cell.
cards.quote: So both get the same full set as the parent: one of every chromosome.

cards.front: In a model of a healing scrape, cells divide to fill a gap in the skin. The cell-cycle time is made shorter. What happens to the time it takes to fill the gap, and why?
cards.back: In the model, the gap fills faster. Each cell divides more often, so new cells pile up sooner.
cards.quote: Predict how a shorter cell cycle changes the time to fill the gap.
cards.section: Explore: heal a scrape, one cell at a time

cards.front: Why does a snapshot of cells dividing out of step tend to catch more cells in interphase than in mitosis?
cards.back: Interphase usually lasts longer than all of mitosis. The longer a stage lasts, the more cells are in it at any one moment.
cards.quote: so a snapshot of cells dividing out of step tends to catch more in interphase

cards.front: Of 36 photographed onion root-tip cells, 20 were in interphase. What percent of the cells is that?
cards.back: 20 ÷ 36 = 0.556, so about 56% of the cells were in interphase.
cards.quote: Out of 36 photographed onion root-tip cells, 20 were in interphase, more than all four stages of mitosis together (20 cells against 16).

cards.front: Of 36 onion root-tip cells, 20 were in interphase. If one cell cycle takes 24 hours, about how many hours does interphase take?
cards.why: Rule: a stage's share of the cells is taken as its share of the time.
cards.quote: Use the second film's steps: cells ÷ 36, then × 24 hours.

cards.front: Suppose all the cells in a root tip divided at the same time, like a school moving at one bell. Could one photo tell you how long each stage lasts? Why or why not?
cards.back: No. One photo could catch nearly all the cells in one stage and say nothing about time.
cards.why: The share-of-cells rule only works when cells divide out of step.
cards.quote: If they all divided together, like a school moving at one bell, one photo could catch nearly all in one stage and say nothing about time.

cards.front: Give two reasons to treat the onion photo estimate of stage times with caution.
cards.back: Any two: 36 photos is a small sample; the 24-hour cycle is a round number, not a measured time; the photos seem to hold more dividing cells than a real root tip.
cards.quote: Its 24-hour cycle is a round number for the activity, not a measured time
cards.section: Where the onion numbers come from

cards.front: A student tests whether onion roots grow faster in a warm place than in a cool place. Name the independent variable and the dependent variable.
cards.back: Independent variable: temperature (for example near 15 °C and near 25 °C). Dependent variable: root length in millimetres, measured each day.
cards.why: A fair test also keeps other things the same and uses at least 5 onions at each temperature.
cards.quote: Independent variable: temperature, such as a cool spot near 15 °C and a warm spot near 25 °C, checked with a thermometer.

cards.front: Onion roots in the warm group grow longer each day than roots in the cool group. What does this suggest about the cells near the root tip?
cards.back: Temperature may speed up how fast cells near the tip divide and stretch.
cards.why: Roots grow when cells near the tip divide and the new cells stretch.
cards.quote: Faster growth in the warm group would suggest that temperature speeds this up.

cards.front: Compare mitosis and meiosis: how much of the parent's genetic material does each new cell get?
cards.back: Mitosis: the same full set as the parent. Meiosis, which makes sex cells: half the parent's genetic material.
cards.quote: A different kind of division, meiosis, makes sex cells with half the parent's genetic material.
cards.section: One-celled living things and sex cells
